title: Fiscal repair increasingly depends on whether people can understand, contest, and shape budget trade-offs
source_unit: OECD, The People and the Budget: Empowering Public Understanding of Public Finances
geography: OECD countries and public-finance institutions, drawing on 2024-2025 OECD surveys and comparative institutional analysis

four_pillars.value: The report organizes reform capacity around demystifying budgets for decision makers, communicating public finances clearly, fostering genuine citizen engagement, and making independent fiscal institutions proactive public advocates

pressure_context.value: Record debt and spending pressures from cost of living, defence, extreme weather, and ageing make public buy-in more important for difficult trade-offs

observations.method: OECD policy synthesis using the 2025 Survey of Government Communicators, 2025 Survey on Parliamentary Budget Oversight, 2024 OECD Trust Survey, and 2024 Fiscal Advocacy Index.
observations.uncertainty: The four pillars are an institutional diagnosis and reform framework, not evidence that any one communication or participation intervention increases fiscal consent or improves budget outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Citizens, legislators, government communicators, parliamentary budget actors, independent fiscal councils, public budget offices, and audit institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Clearer communication and engagement can improve understanding without resolving distributive conflict; disagreement may reflect real trade-offs rather than an information deficit.

observations.period: 2024; trust, political voice, and fiscal legitimacy

denominator.unit: 2024 OECD Trust Survey cross-country public-opinion frame

low_trust.unit: percent reporting low or no trust in national government

political_voice.unit: percent who feel the political system lets people like them have a say

trust_voice_gap.unit: percentage-point trust gap between people who feel people like them have a say and those who do not

observations.method: OECD interpretation of the 2024 OECD Trust Survey as used in the report's discussion of public buy-in and fiscal communication.
observations.uncertainty: The figures are descriptive survey associations; the reported trust gap should not be read as a causal estimate that voice alone produces trust or fiscal consent.
observations.subgroup: Adults across the OECD Trust Survey countries, differentiated by perceived political voice.
observations.counterinterpretation: Perceived voice may reflect broader institutional performance, identity, material security, or political alignment rather than a separable communication effect.

observations.period: 2026; budget communication in fragmented information environments

communication_route.value: The report recommends plain-language explanations, visual presentation, distribution through media and social platforms, and tracking whether communication reaches and informs intended audiences

information_pressure.value: Fragmented media and polarized online debate make long-term fiscal communication more difficult

observations.method: OECD synthesis of government-communicator survey evidence and comparative public-finance communication practice.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not establish which channels change beliefs, reduce polarization, or alter support for specific budget measures.
observations.subgroup: People with different levels of fiscal knowledge, media access, language access, digital access, and political trust.
observations.counterinterpretation: More communication can increase contestation or selective interpretation when distributive stakes are high; reach is not the same as comprehension or influence.

engagement_scope.value: Genuine citizen engagement is framed as extending beyond elections into budget understanding, deliberation, and opportunities to shape trade-offs

institutional_advocacy.value: Fiscal councils, parliamentary budget offices, and audit institutions are encouraged to use communication platforms and public advocacy to explain fiscal choices

observations.method: OECD comparative fiscal-governance synthesis and institutional recommendations.
observations.uncertainty: The proposed participation and advocacy roles are not an evaluation of whether independent fiscal institutions can remain trusted, neutral, or effective when they become more publicly active.
observations.subgroup: Citizens affected by budget trade-offs, civil-society organizations, legislators, fiscal institutions, and public managers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Participation can be dominated by organized or high-capacity groups, while institutional advocacy may be interpreted as political advocacy and weaken perceived independence.

related_sources.claim: Official OECD DOI and publication citation.

boundary: This record captures an OECD fiscal-communication and democratic-engagement framework plus descriptive trust evidence. It is not a household-incidence analysis, a causal test of communication, or proof that participation resolves distributive conflict or improves fiscal sustainability.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD publication page and report PDF were reviewed for the four-pillar framework, trust and voice figures, communication environment, citizen engagement, and independent fiscal-institution advocacy.
